pronunciation.approximation: gwahn-yin, high level tone on both syllables.
pronunciation.note: Guānyīn 观音 means "Perceiver of Sounds" — the one who hears the cries of the world, a rendering of Avalokiteśvara's name as the Chinese translators analyzed it. The level tone on guān and the falling-level yīn are among the most recognized syllables in East Asian devotion.

domains.title: The One Who Hears
domains.subtitle: Compassion, the Lotus Sūtra, and the Cries of the World
domains.lead: Guānyīn is the most beloved figure of East Asian Buddhism: the bodhisattva who vows to hear every cry of suffering in the world and answer it. Born in India as the male Avalokiteśvara, she became, in China, a mother — and compassion itself found its lasting face.

cards.name: The Lotus
cards.desc: Her seat and symbol: purity flowering unsullied from the mud of the world.

cards.name: The Vase
cards.desc: The pure vase with willow branch — the dew of compassion sprinkled on the suffering.

cards.name: A Thousand Eyes
cards.desc: The thousand-armed form: an eye in every palm — to see and to reach, without limit.

cards.name: Putuoshan
cards.desc: Her island mountain off Zhejiang: the Potalaka of the sūtras, anchored in the Chinese sea.

symbols.name: The willow branch
symbols.meaning: Gentleness that bends and does not break — sprinkled with the dew of mercy

symbols.name: The pure vase
symbols.meaning: The nectar of compassion, poured without end

symbols.name: The child in her arms
symbols.meaning: The Songzi Guānyīn — giver of children, mother of the vow

symbols.name: The white robe
symbols.meaning: The White-Robed and Water-Moon forms of the Song — purity beyond ritual, the sage at ease in the world, reflected in the moonlit water

symbols.name: The crown bearing Amitābha
symbols.meaning: Her origin worn on her brow — the Buddha of the Western Paradise in whose court she serves, and from whom her vow descends

mythology.lead: Guānyīn's "myths" are vows and legends of response: the sūtra promises that whoever calls her name in danger will be heard, Chinese legend supplies the daughter who keeps the promise, and the great novels make her the patron of every journey. What is worshipped is attention itself — the answer that never comes too late.

myths.title: The Universal Gateway
myths.text: Chapter 25 of the Lotus Sūtra — Kumārajīva's Chinese translation of 406 CE, so widely copied on its own that it became the independent Guānyīn Jīng — makes the vow explicit: if beings caught in fire, flood, storm, demon-lands, or the executioner's blade "call in one voice upon the name of Guānshìyīn, the bodhisattva will immediately perceive the sound and free them." The chapter names the perils one by one and then multiplies the rescue: Guānyīn appears in thirty-three forms — monk, king, celestial, even demon-queller — going wherever beings are. It became the most recited chapter in East Asian Buddhism, chanted at funerals and deathbed vigils, and the Great Compassion Dhāraṇī that grew around her cult turned the vow into a chant anyone could carry. The chapter’s insight is structural: compassion is not an emotion but an infrastructure — a cosmic emergency line with no closing hour, answering every call.

myths.title: Miàoshàn of Fragrant Mountain
myths.text: The legend that made her a daughter is preserved in the Xiangshan Baojuan, a precious scroll of the twelfth–thirteenth centuries: Princess Miàoshàn refuses marriage to pursue awakening, and her enraged father commits her to a convent and then burns it down around her. Executed at last, she descends to the underworld — where her compassion turns hell into a garden of flowers, and the kings of death hasten to restore her to life. When the same father lies dying of a karmic disease curable only by the eyes and arms of one without anger, a blind, armless monk appears and gives them. The monk is his daughter. Revealed as the thousand-armed, thousand-eyed Guānyīn, she forgives him, and the king becomes her devotee. The story is pious fiction, not scripture — and it did what scripture could not: it gave East Asia's compassion a daughter's face, and made the most radical of vows imaginable as a family drama every household knew.

myths.title: Avalokiteśvara Comes East
myths.text: The Indian Avalokiteśvara — "the lord who looks down in compassion" — entered China with the first sūtra translations, and Kumārajīva's school analyzed the Sanskrit name into exactly what Chinese could carry: guān, to observe; shì, the world; yīn, its sounds. The early art keeps the Indian body: Tang paintings and Dunhuang banners show a princely, sometimes mustached figure, and Dunhuang manuscripts even depict the pilgrim Xuanzang's celestial guardian as a masculine guide. The transformation came between the late Tang and the Song: by the eleventh century the white-robed woman stands in nearly every temple. Scholars debate the causes — the Miàoshàn legend, the cult of the Queen Mother, the sheer grammar of a culture that heard mercy in a mother's voice. The result is one of the great metamorphoses of religious history: the bodhisattva crossed a continent and changed sex, and the change carried the doctrine further than any translation could.

myths.title: The Pilgrimage's Case Officer
myths.text: In Journey to the West (ch. 8–9), Guānyīn volunteers for the quest that organizes the whole novel: the Buddha offers the scriptures of the Great Vehicle, and she descends to the world of the Tang to find someone worthy to fetch them. She recruits the entire pilgrimage — the monk Tripitaka, the disgraced celestial officer who will be Zhu Bajie, the exiled curtain-lifting general who will be Sha Wujing, and the dragon prince who will serve as a horse — and for Sūn Wùkōng she keeps the golden fillet and the headache spell that turn the monkey from a catastrophe into a disciple (ch. 13–14). Through eighty-one tribulations she returns whenever heaven's bureaucracy stalls, once descending with the fish-basket that gave her another popular form. The novel's theology is plain: the journey works not because the pilgrims are strong but because compassion is their case officer — mercy quietly running the operation from above, one rescue at a time.

lore.syncretism: She is the great syncretist of East Asia: in Tibet she is Chenrezig, patron of the land, incarnate in the Dalai Lamas; in Japan Kannon, with temples from Asakusa to Kiyomizu; in Vietnam Quan Âm. Chinese folk religion fused her with the Queen of Heaven and associated her with Mazu the sea-goddess; Daoism canonized her as Cihang Zhenren; and she entered the Journey to the West as the pilgrimage's divine patron, who recruits the pilgrims and rescues them whenever heaven's bureaucracy fails.
lore.culturalLegacy: Her name is spoken daily by more people than perhaps any other divine name on earth: nāmó Guānshìyīn Púsà is East Asia's universal cry in fear and gratitude. Putuoshan draws millions of pilgrims yearly; her statues — from the Suma temple Kannon to the hundred-metre Guānyīn of the South Sea of Sanya — rank among the largest on earth. Vegetarian mercy, lifesaving charities, and countless hospitals across the Chinese world bear her vow.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Guānyīn is the vow that hearing comes first. Not judgment, not power — attention: the sounds of the world, all of them, answered. She asks the question that closes every sūtra about her: in a world crying out in a billion voices, what does it take to be one who hears?

Her vow scales with the century: more cries than ever, more channels than ever — and the same first requirement. The bodhisattva's thousand arms and thousand eyes are not a fantasy of power but of capacity: to hear without triage, to reach without ranking. Every crisis line, every rescue service, every stranger who simply stays on the phone is her liturgy in action: the sounds of the world, answered one at a time.

In the clinics and charity kitchens of the Chinese world her name functions as a common noun for selfless care — the volunteer is 'a living Guānyīn.' It is the vow's final transformation: from cosmic bodhisattva to a standard any person can be measured against. The thousand eyes were never on the statue; they are the world's need, looking back at whoever will answer.

The thousand arms were never a boast; they are the arithmetic of need — a hand for every cry, an eye for every direction the cry comes from. The vow does not scale down; that is why she is asked for everything from safe passage to a child. The bodhisattva of hearing is the proof that attention, fully given, is already help.

lore.archaeology: Putuoshan's three great monasteries (Puji, Fayu, Huiji) preserve her island cult from its 10th-century founding, when a Japanese monk's Kannon image refused to sail on and stayed. Dunhuang's Mogao caves hold her earliest Chinese icons — the guide-of-souls Guānyīn leading the dead, the thousand-armed forms of the Tang. The Northern Song colossal bronze thousand-armed Guānyīn of Longxing Monastery in Zhengding, China, cast in 971 CE, and the Song-dynasty polychrome "Water-Moon Guānyīn" figures — of which the Nelson-Atkins example is the most celebrated — mark her iconography's golden age.
lore.originalScriptNote: Written 观音 in simplified, 觀音 in traditional characters: guān (to observe, with the seeing radical) plus yīn (sound). The fuller liturgical name 观世音 (Guānshìyīn, "Perceiver of the World's Sounds") preserves the whole Sanskrit sense.
